Weariness is a noun that describes a deep, heavy feeling of being tired — not just in your body, but often in your mind and emotions too. It is the state of being weary.

Think of it this way: when you have done something for a very long time, or when life has been difficult and demanding for a long stretch of time, and you feel like you have no more energy left — not just to move, but even to care or to think — that feeling is weariness.

It is not the light tiredness you feel after a short walk. It is heavier. It settles over you like a weight.

Weariness can live in three places:

1. The body. After carrying heavy bags for hours, or after a long journey on foot, your muscles ache, your limbs feel like stone, and even sitting up feels like an effort. That physical heaviness is weariness. You might see phrases like "a bone-deep weariness" — meaning the tiredness has gone all the way to your bones, your very core.

2. The mind. When you have been thinking hard, worrying constantly, or solving problems without a break, your mind grows foggy and slow. You cannot concentrate. Even reading a simple sentence takes effort. This is mental weariness.

3. The emotions. This is perhaps the most important and distinctive form. When you have been dealing with the same painful situation again and again — a difficult relationship, repeated failures, years of struggle — your heart grows tired. You feel worn out, not just physically, but inside. You may feel a loss of hope, a loss of enthusiasm, or a dull resignation. That is emotional weariness.

Often, weariness combines all three at once.
The Key Character of Weariness: It Builds Over Time

One of the most important things to understand about weariness is that it is not sudden. You do not become weary in a moment. It accumulates — it builds up slowly, over days, weeks, or even years of effort, hardship, or monotony.

This is what separates weariness from simple tiredness. Tiredness is what you feel after one tiring day. Weariness is what you feel after a hundred of them.

Imagine a soldier who has been in a war for three years. He is not just tired from last night. He is weary of the fighting, the fear, the loss. That is why we have the phrase war weariness — the exhaustion a whole nation or army feels after prolonged conflict.

Weariness is often directed at something — a particular thing that you are tired of. The structure is "weariness of [something]".

  • A weariness of routine — being tired of doing the same thing every day
  • A weariness of disappointment — being worn down by repeated letdowns
  • A weariness of the world — feeling tired of life, people, and all its troubles in general

This last one — world-weariness — is a compound word with its own specific meaning: a deep, philosophical tiredness with life and human existence itself. A world-weary person has seen too much, been disappointed too many times, and no longer feels wonder or excitement about anything.
How It Feels: The Inner Quality

What makes weariness special as a word is that it carries a certain heaviness of spirit. When someone experiences weariness, there is often:

  • A longing for rest — not just sleep, but relief from whatever is causing the burden
  • A feeling of having given all you can — as if the well is dry
  • Sometimes, a quiet resignation — a low-level acceptance that things are hard and will continue to be
  • A slowing down — movements, speech, and thinking all become slower and heavier

You might see a character in a story described as speaking "with weariness in his voice" — meaning his voice is flat, slow, and heavy, drained of energy and emotion.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close in meaning, but not identical:

Tiredness is the most ordinary, everyday word. It is light and common. You can be tired after one bad night's sleep. It is usually temporary and easily fixed.

Fatigue is more serious and is often used in medical, scientific, or formal contexts (muscle fatigue, compassion fatigue, battle fatigue). It suggests a measurable depletion of energy, physical or mental.

Exhaustion is at the extreme end — a total and complete running out of energy. If weariness is a tank running low on fuel, exhaustion is the tank being completely empty.

Weariness sits between these, but it is different from all of them in one crucial way: it is the most emotional and spirit-level word. It suggests not just a lack of energy, but a heaviness of the soul, a wearing away of a person over time. It is also more literary and formal in tone — you will encounter it more in books, essays, and thoughtful writing than in casual spoken conversation.

Here are natural ways weariness appears in sentences:

  • "A deep/profound weariness settled over her." — meaning: the feeling came and weighed heavily on her
  • "He spoke with weariness." — meaning: his voice showed how tired and worn-out he was
  • "There was a weariness in his eyes." — meaning: his eyes showed exhaustion and perhaps sadness
  • "She felt a sudden weariness." — meaning: the feeling came upon her quickly
  • "Weariness crept into his bones." — meaning: tiredness slowly took over his entire body
  • "The weariness of years of hardship." — meaning: the accumulated tiredness from long suffering

Weariness is a moderately formal and literary word. In everyday spoken English, most people would simply say "I'm so tired" or "I'm exhausted." But in writing — novels, poetry, essays, news articles, speeches — weariness is a natural and powerful choice because it carries emotional weight and depth that "tiredness" does not.

If someone says "I'm tired of this," it is casual and direct. But if someone says "There is a weariness in him that no amount of sleep can cure," it tells us something deeper — that the tiredness is in the soul, not just the body.
A Final Image to Remember It By

Picture an old farmer who has worked the same hard land for forty years. His back aches, his hands are rough, the harvests have been poor, and the work never ends. When you look at him, you see it in his face, in the slowness of his movements, in the quiet way he looks at the horizon. He is not just tired from today. He is weary. That look — that deep, accumulated, body-and-soul heaviness — is weariness.
